ACL: rules and evaluation order: An ACL compares the packet against rules based on source, destination, protocol, and ports. Order matters: the first matching rule determines the result. A conventional ACL does not track the entire connection like a stateful firewall; return traffic may need its own rules.
A general deny rule placed before a specific exception prevents the exception from being used.
Compare the applied rule and its counters with the packet.
Test outbound and return traffic after changing the ACL order or interface.
Rules and blocks are applied along the packet path, including NAT decisions when configured.

NAT rewrites addresses between networks; PAT also uses ports to distinguish connections that share an outside address. The translation table allows the reply to be forwarded to the original host. NAT depends on routes and does not replace a security policy.
Two PCs can reach the same server using a single outside IP, with different translated ports.
Compare the address and port before and after translation.
Check the NAT entry and the return path to the original host.
Translations, expiration, and hairpinning are part of the lab state.
Stateful firewall and application inspection

A stateful firewall tracks the state of flows and can tell replies apart from new connections. Zone policies control paths between networks. Application inspection uses data such as the HTTP Host/path or the DNS name to make decisions, in addition to addresses and ports.
Two requests to the same TCP/80 server can have different results because they use different Host names.
Compare sessions, zones, and the rule that permitted or blocked the flow.
Change only the HTTP Host and check the inspection decision.
Inspection examines supported protocols in cleartext; it does not decrypt external applications.

An IDS detects behaviors and signatures and logs alerts. An IPS can also block the matching traffic. High rates can trigger a rule even without a signature in the payload. An alert describes a match against the rule, not proof of an attack on a real network.
A rate rule can raise an alert in the IDS and drop the same flow when configured for prevention in the IPS.
Compare signatures, threshold, and alert counters.
Repeat the traffic in detection and prevention modes and observe the drops.
Rules and signatures are limited to the content of the modeled packets.
NETCONF/RESTCONF and remote configuration

Management protocols let you query and change the configuration over the network. In NETCONF, candidate keeps a proposed change separate from the running configuration; validate checks the proposal and commit applies it. RESTCONF uses HTTP resources and can control concurrency with ETags. Connectivity and authorization are still required.
Editing candidate does not change forwarding immediately; the effect appears after a successful commit.
Compare candidate and the running configuration before and after the commit.
Check the job response and test access without proper authorization.
XML/framing and HTTP resources are modeled with a limited set of configurations.
SNMP, syslog, and telemetry

Monitoring observes the network without having to read each device's screen. SNMP polls values, syslog sends event logs, and telemetry publishes sensor measurements. Missing data may indicate a failure on the path to the collector, not a lack of activity on the device.
An interface can transmit frames while the collector receives no samples because an ACL blocks their delivery.
Compare local counters with the data received by the collector.
Break the path to the collector and check queries, messages, and timeouts.
Collectors, events, and sensors are inside the simulated topology.
NTP and clock synchronization

NTP exchanges timestamps to estimate the delay and clock offset between client and server. The client selects usable references and adjusts its offset. Stratum indicates the logical distance to a reference; a low number alone does not confirm that the server is reachable or correct.
A device with a high offset can correct it after receiving replies from a configured server.
Compare offset, delay, stratum, and the selected server.
Disable the server and watch for loss of synchronization.
The adjustment uses virtual time and does not change the clock of the computer or operating system.
PoE and power budget

PoE supplies power over the Ethernet link. The power source is the PSE and the consumer is the PD. Class, standard, and available power must match. A switch with an exhausted budget can leave a device without a power feed even when the data cable is connected.
Two APs can compete for the switch's budget; priority determines which one stays powered.
Compare class, consumption, reserved power, and total budget.
Increase consumption or reduce the budget and observe the dependent devices.
Power and negotiation are model values, with no physical electrical effects.

A point-to-point serial link requires compatible settings and a clock source. The DCE side provides the clocking used by the DTE. The clock rate limits transmission. IP traffic between the two ends does not use ARP as it would on an Ethernet LAN.
Two enabled interfaces may fail to exchange data if neither end provides the required clock.
Compare DCE/DTE roles and speed on both ends.
Send traffic and observe serialization and frame checking.
The engine uses a simplified HDLC envelope and FCS check.
Console and local access

A console connection provides terminal access without depending on an IP address, gateway, or route. The ports and serial speed must be compatible. This path is useful for configuring a device before network connectivity exists.
A router without an IP address can receive commands over the console from a device connected to its console port.
Connect console ports with a compatible baud rate.
Run a command on the remote device and check the resulting configuration.
The console operates inside the lab; it does not open a real serial port on the computer.
MTU and IPv4 fragmentation

The MTU limits the size of a packet that fits on a link. IPv4 can fragment a larger packet, and the destination must reassemble it. With DF set, the router does not fragment and may respond with ICMP Fragmentation Needed. Losing a fragment prevents complete reassembly.
A small ping may succeed while a larger packet fails to cross a link with a smaller MTU.
Compare the packet size and the path MTU.
Resend with and without DF and open the ICMP error or the fragments.
Fragments and reassembly have limits and timers in the engine.

DNSSEC makes it possible to verify the authenticity of records through signatures and a chain of trust; it does not encrypt the query. EDNS extends the DNS message format and allows capabilities to be advertised, such as a larger UDP limit. A large or truncated response may require TCP transport.
An invalid signature can cause the resolver to reject a record even if the server answers the query.
Compare the signature, trust, and validation result.
Change EDNS limits and check truncation and retry over TCP.
DNSSEC uses the simulator's own signed representation, without validating real Internet zones.

A proxy receives a request from the client and opens another connection to the destination server. These are two separate flows, each with its own routes, TCP states, and policies. The client reaching the proxy does not guarantee that the proxy can reach the server.
The request reaches the proxy, but access fails because the destination is not allowed or its route is missing.
Compare the client–proxy connection with the proxy–server connection.
Change the list of allowed destinations and check the HTTP result.
The proxy handles the lab's HTTP subset and does not browse the Internet.
Load balancer

A load balancer receives requests on a common entry point and chooses a destination server. Round-robin alternates between destinations and least-connections considers active connections. Health checks help remove unavailable servers; they also need connectivity to each backend.
New requests may go to the second server after the first one fails its health check.
Compare the algorithm, the backends, and their health status.
Disable a server and observe the destination chosen for new requests.
Selection and health checks use simulated HTTP connections.
IP phone, SIP, and RTP

SIP signals call setup and teardown. SDP describes media parameters, and RTP carries the audio in a separate stream. Completing signaling does not guarantee that the media path works in both directions.
A call can be accepted and still have no audio if media datagrams are blocked.
Compare the SIP state with the addresses and ports negotiated for RTP.
Break the media path and check the call result.
The lab models signaling and PCMU samples without calling an external phone.
IP printer and IPP

A network printer receives jobs through an IP service. IPP, carried over HTTP, lets you submit, query, and cancel jobs. The queue can accept a request and still be waiting for paper or processing; connectivity and print completion are different states.
A job enters the spool but stays pending when the printer runs out of paper.
Submit a job and check its status in the queue.
Change paper availability and track completion or cancellation.
Pages, queue, and paper are simulated; no print job is sent to a real device.

MQTT connects clients to a broker. A client publishes messages to topics and others receive them through subscriptions. Wildcards select families of topics, and a retained message can be delivered to a new subscriber. The sensor does not need to know the address of each consumer.
A sensor publishes to room/temperature and a client subscribes to room/# to receive its measurements.
Compare published topics, subscriptions, and received messages.
Reconnect a subscriber and check retained messages and keepalive.
The engine implements an MQTT 3.1.1 subset for the lab's clients and brokers.
Database service over the network

A client must reach and authenticate with the service before querying data. The transport carrying the request to the server does not guarantee that the query is valid or allowed. Separating network, authentication, and query failures makes it easier to identify the cause of an error response.
The server may respond over HTTP but reject a query because of a wrong key or a nonexistent table.
Compare the connection, access key, and query response.
Change a record and query the table again from the client.
The service provides limited SQL over HTTP/TCP and does not access the app's account database.

IP addresses of the sender and recipient of this datagram.
Protocol / hop limit
The protocol identifies the carried content; TTL limits how many routers the packet can cross.
Message type
Indicates this packet's role in the protocol: discovering neighbors, advertising configuration, testing, or carrying data.
Protection sequence
Number used by the radio protection model to detect replayed messages. It is not the TCP sequence number.
Integrity check
Value used to detect changes to the model's protected content.
Protected payload
Data protected on the wireless link; its recipient needs the matching association and key.
MPLS label stack
The outermost label is evaluated first. Each label includes a hop limit and a traffic class.
Encapsulated packet
Content carried inside the encapsulation; it is not the outer network header.
Encapsulated Ethernet frame
Virtual network frame carried inside the VXLAN tunnel.
STP domain / instance
Identifies the set of VLANs or the instance in which this root election takes place.
Packet that caused the error
Part of the original packet returned in the ICMP message so the sender can identify the affected operation.
Sequence of the packet that caused the error
Ties the ICMP message to the original TCP segment.
Where this record was produced; not necessarily the original source of the packet.
Port or radio related to the record. General changes may not have a specific interface.
Source MAC
Identifies the interface that sent the frame on this link.
Destination MAC
Indicates who should receive the frame; ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff is broadcast, addressed to everyone on the link.
Source IP
Address of the host that originated this IP packet.
Destination IP
Address that routing must reach.
Address of this packet's source.
Address the packet is headed to.
Source port
Identifies the sending endpoint of the transport communication. It is not a physical port.
Identifies the receiving endpoint; it often corresponds to the requested service.
SYN opens the connection; ACK acknowledges; FIN closes one direction; RST aborts the connection.
TCP sequence
Number of the first data byte in this segment. SYN and FIN also consume a sequence number.
TCP acknowledgment (ACK)
Next sequence number expected by the receiver; acknowledges receipt of the previous bytes when ACK is present.
Receive window
Number of bytes the receiver advertises it can accept beyond the ACK; it is not the sender's congestion window.
TTL — hop limit
Decremented at each router; when it reaches zero, the packet is dropped to limit loops.
IPv6 hop limit
Decremented at each router; serves the same purpose as the IPv4 TTL.
Network name (SSID)
Advertised name of the Wi-Fi network; it does not identify a client and is not the password.
Advertised security
Indicates how access is protected. An open network does not require key-based authentication.
Message
Control step or type carried in this packet.
Type of request, response, or notification in this protocol.
Negotiation identifier
Correlates the steps of the same access attempt in this model.
Single-use value (nonce)
Value used in the authentication handshake to tell exchanges apart and reduce message replay.
Payload protection
Identifies the algorithm represented by the simulation; it does not prove production-grade encryption.
Ethernet payload type
Indicates the protocol carried by the Ethernet frame.
Encapsulation
Indicates how the control protocol is carried in the frame.
VLAN identification
The tag identifies a VLAN on a trunk link. Without a tag, the VLAN depends on the port configuration.
STP root identity
Priority and MAC used to identify the elected root switch.
Cost to root
Accumulated path cost; STP compares costs to choose ports.
Switch identity
Priority and MAC of the switch advertising this BPDU.
Port identity
Identifies the port that advertised the BPDU and is used in tie-breaking.
Message age
Accumulated time used to limit how long STP information remains valid.
Topology change
Signals a path change; it can cause MAC table entries to be updated or aged out.
RSTP proposal / agreement
Flags used to coordinate a safe port transition. 1 means set; 0 means not set.
ARP operation
Request asks for the MAC of an IPv4 address; reply returns the mapping to the requester.
Sender IPv4
Address of the host providing or requesting the ARP mapping.
Target IPv4
Address whose MAC is being resolved on the local network.
IPv4 identification
Links fragments of the same datagram for reassembly.
Fragment offset
Position of the data in the original datagram, expressed in 8-byte units.
More fragments?
True means this is not the last fragment of the datagram.
Packet size
Modeled length, in bytes.
Size
Modeled length, in bytes; the content may occupy only part of it.
ICMP type / code
Distinguishes a test message from an error and indicates the reported condition.
Test identifier
Matches an ICMP reply to the corresponding request.
Transaction ID
Matches the request and response of the same operation.
DNS question
Name and record type the client wants to look up.
Recursion desired
Indicates whether the client asked the server to find an answer on its behalf.
DNS response code
NOERROR means the query was processed without error; NXDOMAIN means the name does not exist. A response without an error may still not contain the requested record.
Authority / recursion / truncation
AA: authoritative answer; RA: recursion available; TC: truncated response. 1 means set; 0 means not set.
DHCP client MAC
Identifies the interface requesting the configuration.
Current client IPv4
May be 0.0.0.0 while the client does not have an address yet.
DHCP relay address
Identifies the network served by the agent that relays the request to the server.
